# 1 Clement Chapter 40 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 1 Clement 40 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/1CL_040_page_001.jpg

---

## Chapter 40

**40:1** Since therefore these things are plain to us, and we have looked into the depths of divine knowledge, we ought to perform in orderly fashion all the things that the Master has commanded us to do at their appointed times.

**40:2** He ordained that offerings and ministrations should be performed — not carelessly or in disorder, but at fixed times and seasons.

**40:3** Both where and through whom he willed them to be performed, he himself determined by his supreme will: so that all things being done in holiness according to his good pleasure might be well-pleasing to his will.

**40:4** Those therefore who present their offerings at the appointed times are accepted and blessed; for following the ordinances of the Master they do not go astray.

**40:5** For to the high priest his own liturgical duties have been assigned; to the priests their own proper place has been appointed; upon the Levites their own ministries have been laid; the layman is bound by the regulations for laymen.

---

## Translator's Note

Chapter 40 is the hinge of Clement's argument from ordered OT worship to ordered Christian ministry. The argument moves in four steps: (1) God has commanded everything to be done in order (v. 1); (2) OT offerings had divinely appointed times and procedures (v. 2); (3) God himself determined the where and how of proper worship (v. 3); (4) therefore those who follow the appointed order are acceptable to God (v. 4). Verse 5 then enumerates the OT hierarchy — high priest, priests, Levites, laity — as the template. The term *laikos* (layman) in v. 5 is the first attested use of this word in Christian literature. The chapter sets up the parallel argument in chs. 41-44 that Christian communities have an analogous divinely-appointed order: bishop/overseer, deacon, congregation.

---

*SOPHIA represents the consensus translation, balancing literalness and clarity.*
